PHSCS 587

Nanowire and gate-all-around electrostatics

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a surrounding gate controls a cylindrical silicon channel through a coaxial oxide

A gate surrounding a thin wire controls its potential from all azimuthal directions. Low mobile charge can occupy much of the body; at stronger inversion the distribution can move toward the perimeter. Better geometric control does not remove confinement or tunneling limits.

For ideal concentric cylinders, oxide capacitance per channel length is Cₒₓ,L = 2πεox / ln[(R + tox)/R], with units F/m. This differs from planar oxide capacitance per area, εox/tox in F/m². Charge and current equations must use matching dimensional quantities.

Using electron inversion charge per length Qinv,L < 0, the long-channel drift expression is ID = −μeff Qinv,L dV/dy under a consistent current convention. A realistic nanoscale calculation may require quantum populations, contact effects and transport beyond constant-mobility drift.

Example

For an illustrative SiO₂ permittivity 3.9ε₀, R = 5 nm and tox = 1 nm, the ideal coaxial oxide capacitance is about 1.19 × 10⁻⁹ F/m, or 1.19 fF/μm. It is not the total measured gate capacitance of a complete device.

Practice

1. Why is substituting a sheet charge in C/m² directly into the wire current equation dimensionally wrong?

Multiply the units of mobility, charge and potential gradient.

μ has m²/(V·s) and dV/dy has V/m. A line charge in C/m yields C/s = A; a sheet charge leaves an extra inverse length. Geometry must convert it to charge per channel length first.
